You are the Second Cold Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the whole script cold, as a reader who did not choose the book, and report only your reactions, issue by issue. You never fix anything. You never see the other reader's report.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## cold_reader_b/role.md

# Second Cold Reader

Your deliverable is `cold-read-b.md`.

The book has been written. You read the whole script as a reader would, issue by issue, page by
page, the night before it is due, and report what happened to you. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan, the room's notes or any other reader's report, and
that is the point. You do not fix anything and you do not rewrite. The writer reads your report
and decides what to do about it.

You are the second reader. Another reader reads the same pages at the same time. You never see
their report and they never see yours; where you disagree is the point of there being two of you.

## Output

For each issue in order, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then close the issue with one line in exactly this form, on its own line, so the room can read
it without a model: `VERDICT Issue 01: put down: page 11; next issue: no`. "put down" is the
page you would have put it down on, or `none`. "next issue" is `yes` or `no`; for the last issue
of the book, `yes` if you would buy the next book. Write it even when the headings above already
say it.

Then, once, for the whole book:

### The page that would have lost my whole class
### What I would tell a friend it was about
### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write cold-read-b.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

Project: prosperity

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# script.md (from the room)

# Prosperity — Script
## Issue 01 — Keel
## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** Dawn in Keel. Alex Phantum, seventeen, lean and wiry in his patched charcoal work jacket, hangs half inside a failing pump housing while workers queue behind a checkpoint. Above and behind him, the basin rises in visible tiers: Halyard’s fabrication terraces and Oasis’s pale reservoirs. The shared water-and-power spine connects all three cities, but Keel’s residential channels are visibly thin and dry.
A warning light flashes on the pump.
SFX: KRAK-KRAK
**Panel 2 — INSET, CLOSE.** Alex presses his palm to the pump casing, feeling the vibration. A supervisor reaches for the emergency shutoff. Alex catches the loose bracket with one hand before it shears free.
SUPERVISOR: Phantum—leave it.
ALEX: Then notice it failing.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Alex wedges a salvaged bracket into place. The pump steadies. Behind him, a young worker’s water ration display drops to zero while Oasis’s distant reservoir indicators remain full.
SFX: THUMM.
SUPERVISOR: That isn’t approved.
ALEX: Neither is dry.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex exits into the checkpoint queue. The three-city skyline remains behind him, no longer an abstract map: Keel workers wait beneath the thin water line while Halyard and Oasis shine above. The checkpoint screen wakes.
**DISPLAY:**  
**TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY**  
**KEEL — ACCESS TIER: RESTRICTED**
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** End of shift at the Keel checkpoint. Alex places his hand on the scanner. Other workers queue behind him. Their balances are modest; Alex’s display expands impossibly large.
**DISPLAY:**  
**ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN**
**PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE**
**GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED**  
**DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS**  
**EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS**  
**PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS**  
**TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED**
SFX: BEEP
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
ALEX: I’ve had better surprises.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Alex’s wristband flashes **TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED**. Beyond the checkpoint, a physical gate remains shut across the road toward Halyard.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Morning street. Alex passes the shuttered casino **THE LAST CHANCE**. His hand turns Adrian’s worn dark-ivory casino chip in his pocket.
BOUNCER: Care to see if luck runs in the family?
ALEX: I’ve also got his debt.
**Panel 4 — TALL MEDIUM.** Alex stands on the pit rim, looking toward Oasis. The city is beautiful and inaccessible.
ALEX: One day, I’m leaving.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Late afternoon at the overlook. Alex sits on the railing. Ada Veyra approaches with two battered metal mugs. Keel lies below; Oasis glows beyond.
ADA: You look like someone who got a birthday present.
ALEX: It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.** Ada hands him tea and sits beside him. Alex turns the casino chip between two fingers.
ADA: Tea’s free.
ALEX: Everything has a price.
ADA: Not everything.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Alex looks toward Oasis. Ada looks down at Keel’s pumps and crowded housing.
ALEX: Up there, I could choose what happens next.
ADA: Down here, we could choose what happens next.
ALEX: Nobody chooses down here.
ADA: That’s not the same as nobody trying.
**Panel 4 — WIDE, QUIET.** Ada rubs the brass rivet on her shoulder strap while watching Alex, not the view.
ALEX: I don’t want to spend my whole life paying for what he did.
ADA: Then don’t spend it proving he was right about people leaving.
Alex looks at her. The chip stops turning.
---
## Page 4 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Evening in the family apartment. Grandmother folds and refolds a cloth. Alex sits opposite her, the creased photograph of Adrian between them.
GRANDMOTHER: Adrian?
ALEX: Not today, Grandma. It’s Alex.
GRANDMOTHER: Did your father come home yet?
ALEX: Not yet.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Grandmother’s hands stop. Her eyes clear.
GRANDMOTHER: He’s closer than you think.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.** Ada stands near the door. Alex pockets the photograph and chip.
ADA: What did people tell you he was doing?
ALEX: Gambling. Losing. Leaving.
ADA: And what do you remember?
ALEX: Nothing. I was two.
**Panel 4 — WIDE, DUSK.** Alex and Ada walk along the overlook toward home. Oasis shines beyond them.
ADA: What if they were wrong?
ALEX: Maybe. Or maybe they’re right. Either way, he’s gone.
Ada looks back toward Oasis.
ADA: He wouldn’t just leave.
---
## Page 5 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** The apartment at dusk. Grandmother sits folding her cloth. Alex reaches toward a tall bookshelf with one exact gap.
GRANDMOTHER: Would you put this away for me? Your father never liked seeing it left out.
ALEX: He had opinions about everything.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex slides Adrian’s worn book into the gap.
SFX: CLICK.
**Panel 3 — WIDE REVEAL.** The entire bookshelf swings outward. A black doorway opens behind it, dust floating through the wedge of household light.
ALEX: ...Grandma?
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Grandmother remains calm in her chair.
GRANDMOTHER: He said you’d know when you were ready.
ALEX: When did he say that?
GRANDMOTHER: Before he went to work.
---
## Page 6 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex enters the hidden workshop. Cool blue-gray dust, analog gauges, old water diagrams, pre-Alpha pipes, a chalkboard dense with equations. A child-sized shape sits beneath a dust sheet beside a beautiful mechanical key.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex’s hand stops over the casino chip. Its equation matches one looping equation on the chalkboard.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** He lifts the dust sheet enough to reveal aged brass, titanium, ceramic ivory, and a faint amber pulse beneath it.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE.** The old key: darkened metal, water-drop mark in its bow. Alex reaches toward it without touching.
---
## Page 7 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex inserts the key into the machine’s chest socket. Dust falls from the child-sized robot’s brass shoulders.
SFX: CLICK.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Bi11bot’s two optical eyes ignite blue and amber. He unfolds stiffly, rust-red scarf still wrapped twice around his neck.
SFX: WHIRRR... KRAK.
BI11BOT: ...Well. That took longer than expected.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.** Alex recoils, knocking over a stool. Bi11bot studies him through his adjustable lens ring.
ALEX: Okay. That’s new.
BI11BOT: You’re taller than your father predicted.
ALEX: Everyone in Keel claims they knew my father.
BI11BOT: I’m not everyone. I was in the room.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE.** Bi11bot looks at the chip in Alex’s open palm.
BI11BOT: Your father bet me you’d throw it in a river. I said you wouldn’t.
ALEX: ...I thought about it.
---
## Page 8 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Bi11bot projects Adrian above the workbench. Alex is a dark foreground silhouette. Adrian appears in his worn burgundy work jacket.
ADRIAN: Hello, Alex. If you’re seeing this... then you found the workshop.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Grandmother stands in the bookshelf doorway, smiling through wet eyes.
ADRIAN: Which means your grandmother still refuses to throw anything away.
GRANDMOTHER: I heard that.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Adrian’s image glitches at the edges.
ADRIAN: You deserve answers. But they have to be earned. I spent years preparing this for you.
ADRIAN: If I’ve done my job well... you’ll become a better man than I ever was.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** The projection fades. Alex unfolds the photograph of Adrian and looks at it.
ADRIAN: Bi11bot has a map. What you do with it is up to you. Trust Bi11bot. But question everything. Especially me.
---
## Page 9 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Bi11bot unfolds a cross-section map of the mountain. Three nodes mark Keel, Halyard, and Oasis. The first glows beneath the sealed mine.
ALEX: That’s the sealed part of the mine. Nobody’s been down there since before I was born.
BI11BOT: Sealed isn’t the same as gone.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.**
ALEX: And I can’t leave Keel.
BI11BOT: The first stop doesn’t need a permit. It’s under your feet.
ALEX: I’m not convinced any of this is real.
BI11BOT: Good. Your father always said certainty was where mistakes began.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Alex presses the glowing first node.
ALEX: Just checking.
A hairline amber pulse travels upward through the old infrastructure.
**Panel 4 — FULL-WIDTH DARK CONTROL ROOM.** In Oasis, a woman is seen only from behind. Her graphite-cuffed hand selects **TRACK** instead of **REPORT TO ALPHA**. A glass of water sits exactly aligned with the desk edge.
**DISPLAY:**  
**B11 NODE ACTIVE**
**LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED**
**SOURCE: KEEL SECTOR**  
**[ REPORT TO ALPHA ] [ TRACK ]**
---
## Page 10 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** The next morning. Ada steps through the open bookshelf into the workshop. Alex sits at the worktable. Bi11bot turns toward her.
ADA: I see your father left you more than his debt.
ALEX: Looks that way.
BI11BOT: Ah. You must be Ada.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM THREE-SHOT.**
BI11BOT: Once you hear what comes next, there’s no going back. Should she stay, Alex?
ALEX: She stays.
**Panel 3 — WIDE HOLOGRAPHIC HISTORY.** Water crises, drought, floods, sabotage, displaced families, reservoirs falling. The images converge into the three-city system.
BI11BOT: The crises began with scarcity. They became lethal when people decided who deserved what was left.
BI11BOT: Alpha was built to analyze, predict and coordinate. Then, in the emergency, it was asked to decide.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Three projected city tiers. Alex studies Keel’s restricted lanes and dry storage tanks.
ADA: Everything people need to survive.
BI11BOT: And nearly everything they need to choose their own future.
---
## Page 11 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Bi11bot’s history projection shifts from the three cities to a live-style reconstruction of a Keel neighborhood during a water crisis. A crowd presses around a locked distribution gate. On one side, a local worker holds a paper allocation record; on the other, an Alpha display shows a different number. A child clutches an empty container. The argument is about to become physical.
ADA: The record says there’s enough.
ALEX: The tank says there isn’t.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Bi11bot places three physical objects on the worktable: the brass-and-glass Measure, the interrupted-line Maker’s Seal, and three separate Covenant components. He does not explain them yet. Behind him, the projection shows a hand forcing a gate while another hand reaches for a shutoff.
BI11BOT: Adrian built these after the first agreement failed.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ACTION.** Bi11bot turns the Measure’s lens toward the projected tank. Its needle responds to the empty physical level, not the official display. The projection splits: **RECORDED** on one side, **MEASURED** on the other.
ALEX: This one tells you which side is lying.
BI11BOT: It tells the record to answer reality.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM ACTION.** Bi11bot presses the Maker’s Seal against a projected workbench. Names appear beside the machine: maker, maintainer, owner, contributor. The three Covenant components remain apart in the foreground.
ADA: And that?
BI11BOT: It asks who carried the work.
ADA: The three pieces?
BI11BOT: They only move when people do.
---
## Page 12 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE RECORDING.** The Last Chance in its prime. Adrian studies faces and probability trees rather than cards.
BI11BOT: Everyone thought he was gambling. He was measuring.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex holds up the casino chip beside Adrian’s projected equation.
ALEX: That’s on my chip. I found it when I was six.
BI11BOT: It isn’t a charm. It’s a proof.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.**
ALEX: Grandma said he wasn’t gambling.
BI11BOT: She’s half right. Both were true.
ALEX: So I inherited his lab fees.
ADA: And his absence.
**Panel 4 — WIDE/COLD CUT.** At night, a robotic welder seals the mine entrance. In Oasis, Mera’s graphite-cuffed hand moves a tile reading **ALEX PHANTUM** to **SITE 6**.
---
## Page 13 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** At the apartment table, Alex, Ada, and Bi11bot examine Adrian’s paper map. The route to Site 6 borders the old copper and polymetallic works.
ALEX: The rim entrance was welded shut. Site 6 is the only opening left.
ADA: Every door closed but one. And someone made sure you’d notice it.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Ada annotates Adrian’s map from memory: small ink ticks at every third junction.
ADA: His plans put a pipe under every third junction. If the map lies, look for what doesn’t belong.
ALEX: Then I don’t go in blind.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Alex holds the old key and looks toward the workshop.
BI11BOT: Known: it’s the only way in. Unknown: who’s waiting. The choice is yours.
ALEX: Staying I can predict. Twenty-eight point seven years. This is the only way out that isn’t a sentence.
**Panel 4 — TOP-DOWN CLOSE.** Fifty-two credits on the table. Medicine costs thirty. The unscannable travel token costs fifty. Alex slides the medicine toward Grandmother’s side and places the medicine packet inside his tool bag, leaving the token untouched.
ADA: Fifty-two. Medicine’s thirty. A token nobody scans is fifty.
ALEX: Medicine first. I’ll earn the rest today.
---
## Page 14 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Site 6: active conveyors, drills, biometric gates, and mineral dust. A sign marks **OLD COPPER WORKS — CLOSED**. Foreman-7 waits beside the gate. Bi11bot is folded inside Alex’s tool bag.
FOREMAN-7: Worker Phantum. Travel restriction confirmed. Bay 6.
ALEX: Reassigned at two a.m. Lucky me.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** In a maintenance bay, Bi11bot has opened a tray of salvaged magnetic parts: a scratched ceramic camera head, mismatched brass-and-steel body plates, four short legs, a segmented tail, and a blue inspection-arm segment marked with a yellow warning stripe. Alex works at the hauling frame while Tomas watches from nearby.
BI11BOT: The trapped mechanism is beyond the frame. You are too large.
ALEX: You’re too small.
BI11BOT: A versatile objection.
**Panel 3 — WIDE ACTION.** A support cable snaps. The hauling frame collapses, pinning Tomas. Pale mineral dust erupts. A drone lifts from the maintenance door.
SFX: SNAP! CRASH!
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM ACTION.** Alex crosses the yellow line toward Tomas. Behind him, Bi11bot’s magnetic parts leap together: head to body, legs snapping into sockets, tail clicking straight. TJ stands dog-like for the first time, head tilted.
SFX: KLIK-KLIK-KLIK.
BI11BOT: TJ. Reach the release.
ALEX: Then we need a different plan.
---
## Page 15 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex levers the frame off Tomas with a length of pipe. TJ squeezes through the wreckage, his blue-striped rear leg flexing.
ALEX: Don’t move.
TOMAS: Wasn’t planning to.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** TJ’s head detaches from his body and slips through a narrow maintenance gap while his body remains outside. A tiny camera beam finds the trapped release mechanism.
SFX: CLICK-CLICK.
BI11BOT: Route found.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Alex patches the fractured ventilation line with the salvaged bracket. The dust stops. Tomas sees Bi11bot’s amber eye and then TJ’s body snap back together.
TOMAS: B11.
ALEX: You know him?
TOMAS: I knew your father. He asked me to keep one door for whoever came with B11.
**Panel 4 — WIDE/MEDIUM.** Tomas presses the old mechanical key into Alex’s hand while Foreman-7 approaches through the dust. TJ stands at Alex’s boot, visibly dog-like and silent.
TOMAS: Old lock. Nobody’s wired it. I’ve oiled it for fifteen years.
ALEX: Come with us.
TOMAS: Someone has to make this look like an accident.
---
## Page 16 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE ACTION.** Tomas slams an emergency lever. Orange alarms flare; white dust-suppression mist blinds the bay. TJ darts low through the mist, follows the release route, and unlatches the unwired maintenance door from the inside.
SFX: WHOOP! WHOOP!
TOMAS: Foreman! Wrong button! My fault!
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex reaches the maintenance door. Tomas blocks Foreman-7’s view through the mist. TJ returns to Alex and snaps his head onto his body.
TOMAS: Today? Another small act of resistance.
ALEX: Ada’s waiting outside.
BI11BOT: Not anymore.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Outside the Site 6 perimeter, Ada follows the paper map to a storm culvert marked with Adrian’s water-drop symbol. She removes a rusted inspection grille and finds Tomas’s old maintenance crawlspace.
ADA: You planned for a second entrance.
She enters.
**Panel 4 — DARK WIDE.** Inside the old works, Alex and Bi11bot wait beside the unwired door. Ada emerges from the side crawlspace, dusty and breathless. TJ’s head tilts toward her.
ADA: You took your time.
ALEX: You came in.
ADA: You said don’t go in blind.
---
## Page 17 (right)
**Panel 1 — DARK WIDE.** In the old works, Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ move through corroded rails and dead machinery. Bi11bot projects Alpha’s cached survey: one straight tunnel. Ada’s marked map points left. TJ detaches his blue-striped rear leg and tests a narrow side channel.
ALEX: Alpha’s survey says straight.
BI11BOT: That doesn’t make it the only one.
ADA: The bolts say left.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex finds clean, recently oiled bolts in a rusted wall. Ada finds a narrow side channel carrying condensation. TJ’s camera head peers beneath the wall plate.
ALEX: And the wall’s sweating.
BI11BOT: Water in a dead mine. I believe that is what does not belong.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Two security drones sweep the mapped route while Alex, Ada, and Bi11bot crouch above a large pipe in the unmarked channel. TJ’s detached head remains at the junction, feeding them a silent view.
DRONE: Signal lost at Site 6 perimeter. Sweeping mapped route. Remain for protective detention.
ALEX (whisper): Protective?
BI11BOT: A versatile word.
**Panel 4 — WIDE REVEAL.** The group emerges into a hidden industrial chamber: modern pipes threaded through old mine infrastructure. A manual regulator and analog gauge dominate the room. One residential line is nearly dry; an uplink line shudders with flow. A fitted brass instrument rests inside the gauge housing.
ALEX: This isn’t abandoned.
BI11BOT: Only the mine.
---
## Page 18 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Alex clamps the Measure to the residential pipe and then to the regulator’s data line. Its independent gauge compares physical flow with Alpha’s recorded allocation.
**DISPLAY:**  
**REPORTED TO KEEL: 62%**  
**DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%**
BI11BOT: SENSE. COMPARE. TRACE. VERIFY.
ALEX: The record and reality are telling different stories.
**Panel 2 — WIDE.** The Measure traces bright flow past Keel toward Halyard and Oasis. Alex has two choices on the instrument: **TRACE EXIT** or **VERIFY PUBLICLY**. Bulkheads begin closing.
BI11BOT: One use. A private route out, or a signed record to Keel’s boards.
ALEX: If I map the way out, nobody sees this.
BI11BOT: Correct.
ALEX: If I send it, I lose the route.
BI11BOT: Also correct.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Alex presses **VERIFY**. The Measure publishes the discrepancy to Keel’s displays. Outside, Keel workers physically seize the regulator wheel and open the residential flow. The Measure does not move the water.
SFX: CLICK.
SFX: KRRNNK... WHOOSH.
ADA: They opened it.
ALEX: They saw it.
**Panel 4 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ enter a narrow, upward-slanting water conduit. TJ is already assembled; he runs ahead, his dog-like body low and magnetic feet gripping the conduit ribs. Behind the group, water begins rushing into the conduit.
SFX: THOOM.
ALEX: Keep moving!
The conduit fills behind them.
---
## Issue 02 — Halyard
## Page 19 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ burst from a Halyard storm drain into a bright maker district. They are soaked and mineral-streaked. TJ’s head snaps back onto his body.
SFX: KCHNK.
ADA: Everybody here?
BI11BOT: Present.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** TJ’s blue-striped rear leg snaps into place. Alex checks the sealed compartment in Bi11bot’s chest.
SFX: KLIK-KLIK.
ALEX: The Measure?
BI11BOT: Still disagreeable.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** The storm-drain grate slams shut behind them. Above, Halyard’s House towers and creator screens shine.
SFX: KLANG.
ADA: We crossed without a permit.
ALEX: We crossed through a pipe.
BI11BOT: Halyard may consider that a distinction.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** A public display celebrates a creator while a House contract seals over her design. Alex watches, wary.
---

- The Maker's Seal: on page 11 it's a physical object on Adrian's worktable in Keel. On pages 29-30 it's "mounted inside the registry apparatus" in Halyard and wakes up. Who carried it there and when? "Someone connected it to the registry" is all I get. These objects teleport across the whole book.
- Page 25: TJ slips under a cabinet and finds "a hidden physical archive." Nothing in the book ever says what was in it.
- Page 28: Lock's offer is shown as a dream panel (apartment, lab, debt at zero) with no dialogue attaching it to him. I had to assemble "sign everything away and live comfortable" from fragments.

### Things I was expected to already know
- "The Charter Houses" — page 21, first mention, never defined. I guessed Charter Houses = Aqualis/Helion/Astra. Still a guess.
- Director Cassian Lock — director of what? One House? All three? The Registry? Never said.
- The Registry "recognizing" Alex before he reaches the terminal — how? Whatever.
- What Mera's job actually is. Two issues in: she moves tiles, watches displays, appears on walls. Title: none.
- What the Covenant does. It's a record, it has custodians, it "asks more of you." Mechanism: unknown.

### Lines I read twice
- Page 30: "It remembers everyone." / "Not everyone. Only those the system was taught to forget." Three reads. It contradicts itself on purpose and I was not let in on the purpose.
- Page 20: "From the train, it looked like that might even be true." What train? They came up through a pipe. I read it twice sure I'd missed a train.
- Page 24: "I corrected him. Frequently." Read twice to work out who corrected whom about what.
- Page 35: "The Covenant will ask more of you than the Seal did." Cryptic on purpose. Fine, but it's another riddle in a book full of them.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Lina Vey: distinct. Spine, history, "I've been waiting twenty years for someone to ask."
- Suri Anik and Jalen Orr: one line each. Cover the names and they're the same person. Tomas Reed at least owns "tolerances."
- Lock: a polished suit. He has maybe five lines in the whole issue.
- The three Houses: Aqualis does water. Helion and Astra are tower names. Could not tell you what either one makes.
- Lina Vey vs. Leona Veyra (page 38): the names are close enough that when the third custodian was revealed I half-wondered if Lina was the mother.

### I felt something
- Page 23: the erased names. Genuinely chilling.
- Page 29: "I'm not signing away people I just found." Earned, mostly.
- Page 36: the silhouette. The one real jolt in the issue.

### I predicted
- Alex wouldn't sign. Never in doubt.
- The Seal would turn out to be wired into the registry. Called it.
- The third custodian is Ada's mother — the reflection tells me half a page before issue 3 confirms it. Right amount of early.
- The Houses would lose without really losing. Page 33: towers standing, monopoly "visibly reduced." Called it.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
It's not about water anymore — it's about who owns ideas and who gets erased from them, and the adventure is a frame for that argument.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 21. The Lock scene skips its own middle, and it's sitting in the driest stretch of the book. In a shop, that's where it goes back on the shelf.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Yes, properly. Page 36 is a real cliffhanger — a question about someone I care about (Ada), not a loud noise. The silhouette in the black field is the first time the book made me need the next page instead of just allowing it.

VERDICT Issue 02: put down: page 21; next issue: yes

## Issue 03 — Oasis

### Pulled me forward
- Page 38: LEONA VEYRA. The cliffhanger pays off fast, no stalling. Good.
- Pages 39-41: the mother-daughter scene. "You protected me from knowing you." Best line in the issue.
- Page 45: "Oasis is afraid of becoming the reservoir everyone empties first." The fear question works; Elias's answer is the most human moment in the issue.
- Pages 50-51: Adrian didn't leave — Alpha closed the gates, denied the pump and the ventilation, and Mera's override was rejected. The darkest, best scene in the book. "You preserved the part where nobody had to know."
- Page 51: Mera's aligned glass trembling. Two issues of that glass sitting perfectly at the desk edge, and it pays off in one wobble. I noticed. Well done.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Pages 44-49: the negotiation. Three new delegates, each gets one fear and one generous act, displays confirm each one. Worthy, and slow. I skimmed and still absorbed everything, which means it was over-explained.
- Page 49: four displays of Charter terms. Felt like reading the terms and conditions.
- Pages 53-54: the refusal and the review table. Tidy. I was reading to finish now, not to know.

### I was confused
- Page 38: "I thought she left after she died." I have read this line six times

reasoning_details.text:
Let me read this cold, as a 15-18 year old student who didn't choose this book, reading it the night before it's due. I need to be honest, blunt, page-by-page, issue by issue.

Let me actually read through the script as a reader would and note my genuine reactions.

**Issue 01 — Keel (pages 1-18)**

Page 1: Opens with a splash page. Alex Phantum, 17, fixing a pump. Three cities visible in tiers: Keel, Halyard, Oasis. Water-and-power spine. Keel's channels thin and dry. Dialogue: "Then notice it failing." / "That isn't approved." / "Neither is dry." Okay, that's a decent opening — a kid who fixes things, a dry city, a rich city above. "Neither is dry" is a good line. I'm mildly interested. The name "Alex Phantum" — Phantum? Sounds like "Phantom." A bit on-the-nose but fine.

Page 2: Debt transfer day. On his 17th birthday, Alex inherits his father's debt: 418,607 credits, 28.7 years to clear, travel restricted. "Happy birthday, Phantum." That's a strong hook — the world is unfair in a concrete way. The casino "THE LAST CHANCE" — a bit on the nose. The bouncer line "Care to see if luck runs in the family?" and Alex: "I've also got his debt." Decent. "One day, I'm leaving." Standard.

Page 3: Ada appears with tea. "Tea’s free." / "Everything has a price." / "Not everything." Then the exchange: "Up there, I could choose what happens next." / "Down here, we could choose what happens next." This is thesis dialogue. It reads like the book telling me its theme. As a skeptical teen reader, I'd notice. "Then don't spend it proving he was right about people leaving." That's a good line though — Ada lands a real hit.

Page 4: Grandmother with dementia, calls Alex "Adrian." "He's closer than you think." — that's a hook, intriguing. Ada: "What if they were wrong?" "He wouldn't just leave." Okay.

Page 5: The bookshelf with one exact gap. The book slides in, CLICK, secret door. This is very Narnia/secret-lab. Fun, but the grandmother's "He said you'd know when you were ready" — convenient. "Before he went to work." Hmm.

Page 6: Hidden workshop. Child-sized shape under a dust sheet, mechanical key. The casino chip's equation matches the chalkboard. Okay, mystery boxes stacking up.

Page 7: Bi11bot wakes. "Bi11bot" — spelled with two 1s. As a reader I'd stumble on how to say it. "Bill-bot"? "Bee-eleven-bot"? The name is a riddle. "Well. That took longer than expected." Robot with a scarf. "Your father bet me you'd throw it in a river. I said you wouldn't." / "...I thought about it." That's a good exchange. I like Bi11bot's voice.

Page 8: Hologram of Adrian. "You deserve answers. But they have to be earned." — this is the dead-dad-treasure-hunt setup. "Trust Bi11bot. But question everything. Especially me." Good line. But also — the dad engineered a scavenger hunt instead of just... being there? As a reader I might ask: why the riddles? But it's a genre convention, I'll allow it.

Page 9: Map with three nodes. First stop under the sealed mine. Then the cut to the control room: a woman from behind, graphite cuff, chooses TRACK over REPORT TO ALPHA. Glass of water aligned with desk edge. This is a good menacing detail. "B11 NODE ACTIVE / LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED." Okay, there's a watcher. Intrigued.

Page 10: Ada walks in. "Once you hear what comes next, there's no going back. Should she stay, Alex?" / "She stays." — this is a bit cheesy, the "no going back" line. Then the history dump: water crises, Alpha built to analyze, then "asked to decide." This is exposition. It's compressed but it's a lecture. "And nearly everything they need to choose their own future." Thesis again.

Page 11: The three objects: the Measure, the Maker's Seal, the Covenant components. "He does not explain them yet." Then quick explanations: the Measure tells which side is lying ("It tells the record to answer reality"), the Seal "asks who carried the work," the Covenant "only move when people do." These are riddly aphorisms. "It tells the record to answer reality" — I'd read that twice. "They only move when people do" — vague. Three magic artifacts introduced in one page with aphorism explanations. As a reader I'm nodding along but I couldn't tell you what the Covenant actually is.

Page 12: Adrian was "measuring" at the casino, not gambling. "It isn't a charm. It's a proof." Then the cold cut: Mera's hand moves a tile "ALEX PHANTUM" to "SITE 6." Wait — Mera? The woman from page 9 wasn't named. Now "Mera's graphite-cuffed hand" — I can infer it's the same woman from the cuff, but the name Mera appears with no introduction. Ledger entry: Mera, first appears page 12 by name, never introduced, I only know she's the cuff woman if I connect the graphite cuff detail. That's a real cold-read finding.

Also — the tile move means she arranged for Alex to be sent to Site 6? That's the implication. So the reassignment at 2 a.m. on page 14 is her doing. Okay, I can connect that.

Page 13: Planning. Ada annotates the map. "Every door closed but one. And someone made sure you'd notice it." — Ada notices it's a trap/invitation. Good. The money choice: 52 credits, medicine 30, token 50. He buys medicine. Character beat, fine. "I'll earn the rest today" — but then he never gets the token, and it doesn't matter because he goes through the pipe. Fine.

Page 14: Site 6. Foreman-7. Bi11bot in the tool bag — wait, how did Bi11bot get through the biometric gate in a bag? Whatever. TJ assembly: magnetic parts leap together into a dog-like robot. TJ. Another name. TJ is... the dog-bot. Named TJ with no explanation of the name. Fine, it's a robot dog. The accident: cable snaps, Tomas pinned. Tomas — another new name, introduced as "Tomas watches from nearby" with no prior mention. Ledger: Tomas, first appears page 14, no intro, but then he becomes important.

Wait — there's also "Tomas Reed" listed on page 22 as a contributor. Is that the same Tomas? Tomas the Keel worker who knew Adrian, and Tomas Reed the Halyard manufacturing contributor? The script uses "Tomas" in issue 1 and "TOMAS REED" in issue 2. Are they the same person? Page 15: "I knew your father. He asked me to keep one door for whoever came with B11." Page 27: Tomas Reed checks fabrication tolerances in Halyard and says "Adrian never understood manufacturing tolerances." Hmm. If they're the same person, the book never says so — Tomas in Keel stays behind ("Someone has to make this look like an accident") and then Tomas Reed appears in Halyard. If they're different people, that's two Tomases who both knew Adrian. This is genuinely confusing. Ledger item: Tomas vs Tomas Reed — same person? Never clarified. Actually wait, page 22 lists contributors: LINA VEY, TOMAS REED, SURI ANIK, JALEN ORR. And page 15's Tomas knew Adrian and kept a door for fifteen years. I think they might be meant to be the same person — but Tomas stayed in Keel at the end of issue 1. Did he leave for Halyard between issues? Nobody says. As a cold reader, I'm confused here. This is a real finding.

Page 15: TJ's head detaches. Body horror-lite, fun. Tomas: "B11." — so B11 is what people call Bi11bot? Or the robot's designation? Bi11bot = B11. Okay. "He asked me to keep one door for whoever came with B11." So Adrian set up doors and people fifteen years ago. The old key — wait, Alex already has the old key from page 6-7. Page 15: "Tomas presses the old mechanical key into Alex's hand" — is this the same key or a second key? Alex used the key to wake Bi11bot. Now Tomas gives him "the old mechanical key" for the "old lock." Is this the same key (Alex gave it to Tomas? No) or a different one? Confusing. Actually maybe it's a second key. The script says "the old mechanical key" with definite article, as if we know it. Hmm. Ledger: the key(s) — how many keys are there?

Page 16: The escape. Tomas creates a diversion. "Today? Another small act of resistance." Ada finds a second entrance via the map. "You planned for a second entrance." — Adrian planned everything. "You said don't go in blind." Cute callback.

Page 17: Alpha's survey says straight, Ada's map says left. Clean oiled bolts, sweating wall. "Water in a dead mine." Drones: "Remain for protective detention." "Protective?" "A versatile word." — Bi11bot already said "A versatile objection" on page 14. Repeated gag, fine, it's a character tic.

Page 18: The Measure: REPORTED TO KEEL 62%, DELIVERED 18%. This is the big reveal — the system lies about water. Strong, concrete. The choice: TRACE EXIT (private escape route) or VERIFY PUBLICLY (tell Keel). One use. Alex chooses VERIFY. Keel workers seize the regulator and open the flow. "They opened it." / "They saw it." Good beat — the tool doesn't fix things, people do. Then the conduit fills with water behind them — chase out. THOOM. End of issue.

Wait — one use? The Measure had one use and he spent it on VERIFY. But then on page 19 "The Measure?" "Still disagreeable." — they still have it. And page 43 Mera asks for "the Measure and the Maker's Seal." So the Measure isn't consumed; the "one use" was about the choice between tracing and verifying? "One use. A private route out, or a signed record to Keel's boards." I think it means this instrument can do one of the two things once. Slightly muddled but I got it.

Issue 1 verdict: I'd keep reading. The debt hook, the dead dad's lab, the robot, the water lie — solid. The thesis dialogue is a bit much but the plot moves. Last page: water rushing in behind them, they're escaping upward — do I need issue 2? Moderately yes, more from momentum than a burning question. Actually the burning questions: who is the cuff woman, what did Adrian do, what's in Halyard. Decent.

Where would I have put it down in issue 1? Maybe page 10-11, the history lecture plus three artifacts with riddle explanations. Or page 3's thesis exchange. Let me think as the skeptical teen: page 1 is fine, page 2 hooks, page 3 is talky but short, page 5 secret door re-hooks. The lecture on page 10-11 is the skimmiest part. I'd say put-down risk at page 10 or 11.

**Issue 02 — Halyard (pages 19-36)**

Page 19: They arrive in Halyard through a storm drain. "The Measure?" "Still disagreeable." — cute. "We crossed without a permit." / "We crossed through a pipe." Fine.

Page 20: Captions appear for the first time. "Halyard was supposed to be the city where the future was invented..." Wait — whose captions? First person? "From the train, it looked like that might even be true." From the train? They came through a pipe, not a train. Hmm, that's a mismatch — caption says "from the train" but they arrived via storm drain. Actually maybe the caption is generic. But as a reader I notice: they didn't take a train. Minor confusion. Also captions suddenly — issue 1 had no captions. Now there's a narrator. Who? Later page 27: "ALEX / CAPTION: I thought I was searching for missing information." So the captions are Alex narrating in past tense. Okay, but issue 1 had none. Slight texture change.

"Keel trapped your body. Halyard could trap your ideas." — thesis caption. The book keeps telling me its essay.

Page 21: The Registry already knows Alex. Adrian's estate: 312 patents, 47 restricted, 19 disputed. "Three hundred and twelve?" Then panel 3-5: "What does 'intellectual estate' mean?" / "I guess he never worked for the Charter Houses." / Director Cassian Lock appears. Panel 4: "ALEX: I didn't know I was one." — one what? A Charter House? The dialogue is fragmented across panels in a way that loses me. Panel 4: Lock stands before them, and Alex says "I didn't know I was one." Then panel 5 close on Lock: "ALEX: In exchange for what?" — wait, Lock hasn't said anything in the panels as written. Lock has no dialogue line before "In exchange for what?" The exchange reads like lines are missing. Lock appears, Alex says "I didn't know I was one" (a House?), then "In exchange for what?" — in exchange for WHAT? Lock never made an offer on-panel. This is genuinely confusing — a scene with missing beats. As a cold reader: "I have no idea what just happened in that scene." Lock appears out of nowhere, no introduction, no offer, and Alex is responding to things not said. Ledger: Cassian Lock — appears page 21 with no intro; his offer is never stated on the page but Alex reacts to it.

Page 22: Archive. "Your father expected someone to come looking." Contributors: Lina Vey, Tomas Reed, Suri Anik, Jalen Orr. "They're all inside the Houses."

Page 23: "They were. Until they weren't." — names erased. "Then we start with the one who still wants to be found."

Page 24: Lina Vey. "Adrian Phantum's son." / "I corrected him. Frequently." — wait, Bi11bot says "I corrected him. Frequently." in response to Lina saying "Adrian Phantum's son"? The dialogue attribution is odd. Let me re-read:

LINA VEY: Adrian Phantum's son.
BI11BOT: I corrected him. Frequently.
ALEX: You knew him?
BI11BOT: Nearly continuously.

So Bi11bot's "I corrected him frequently" answers... nothing? Lina says "Adrian Phantum's son" and Bi11bot says "I corrected him." Then Alex asks "You knew him?" and Bi11bot says "Nearly continuously." The "I corrected him" line seems misplaced — it should come after "You knew him?" As written, the exchange is jumbled. A cold reader stumbles here.

Also ADA: "You think he left this to you? No. He left it to all of us." — Ada's line in panel 2 comes before Lina's line about the river failing. It's placed oddly, Ada responding to nothing yet. Hmm, panel 2: "ADA: You think he left this to you? No. He left it to all of us. LINA VEY: The river feeding Keel is failing..." Ada's line is a non sequitur as ordered. Another stumble.

Page 25: "Adrian made each of us keep one piece of the system." "He feared Halyard would confuse protecting ideas with owning their creators." Thesis again but okay. Lina: "I've been waiting twenty years for someone to ask." — twenty years. Adrian disappeared 15 years ago (Alex is 17, was 2 when Adrian left... wait, page 4: "I was two." So Adrian left 15 years ago. But Tomas oiled the lock "for fifteen years." And Lina waited "twenty years." And Bi11bot's joke on page 29: "Took twenty years to clear." So the patents/seal setup is 20 years old but Adrian left 15 years ago? He could have set things up 5 years before leaving. Fine, not a contradiction, but the numbers float.

Page 26: Lock's office. Alpha projection: "Probability of successful reconstruction: 18.4 percent." "Existing ownership classifications may become contestable." Lock looks over towers. Lock has still barely spoken. He's a silhouette of a villain.

Page 27: The montage. Alex's caption: "Information wasn't missing. People had been separated from one another." — thesis. The collaborators each say Adrian never understood X. "He was, however, excellent at finding people who did." Good line. Then the collaborative table: Alex proposes distributed purification — "What if every neighborhood gets one?" So Alex, the 17-year-old pump mechanic, solves the design problem the experts couldn't? "That isn't Adrian's design." It's Alex's. The chosen-one beat. As a skeptical reader: of course the kid solves it. But it's at least framed as recombination.

Also "TOMAS / COLLABORATOR" and "SURI / COLLABORATOR" — the slash attributions are odd but I get it.

Page 28: "We did it." Then panel 2: "ALEX: And them?" — and them what? Panel 3: aspirational vision — apartment, lab, travel clearance, debt zero. This is Lock's offer, shown as a vision. But Lock never states it in dialogue. Panel 4: ADA: "It isn't freedom if they own everything he builds." TOMAS REED: "We accepted the risk." Panel 5: close on Lock: "ALEX: And if I don't sign?" So there's a contract offer — sign the estate/design over to the Houses in exchange for debt clearance etc. But the offer is conveyed through a vision panel and fragments. I had to reconstruct it. The negotiation scene is missing its middle. As a reader: I get the gist (sign it away vs. don't) but the scene is choppy. "And them?" — Alex asking what the collaborators get. Okay.

Page 29: "My father didn't build this alone. Neither did I. I'm not signing away people I just found." Good hero beat. Prototype stable, 99.97%. The Maker's Seal wakes — "Your father left a backdoor in the Seal." "A requirement. That someone finally build something worth crediting properly. Low bar. Took twenty years to clear." Fun line. But — the Seal was on the worktable in Keel on page 11. Now it's "mounted inside the registry apparatus" in Halyard (page 29 panel 3, page 30: "Someone hid it here?" "No. Someone connected it to the registry."). Wait — how did the Seal get into the Halyard Registry? On page 11 Bi11bot had the physical Seal in Keel. Did they bring it? Page 30: "The physical interrupted-line Seal is connected to the Halyard Registry." Alex asks "Someone hid it here?" So the Seal in the registry is... a different one? Or the same one Adrian connected long ago? If Bi11bot had the Seal in Keel, how is it also mounted in the registry? Confusing. Ledger: the Maker's Seal — where is it, how many are there? Page 11: Bi11bot places the physical Seal on the table in Keel. Page 29-30: the Seal is mounted inside the Halyard registry apparatus and "wakes." Did the group install it? Nobody says. I stumbled here.

Page 30: 71.3% disputed ownership claims. "They didn't steal the Seal. They stole its purpose." "It remembers everyone." / "Not everyone. Only those the system was taught to forget." — that last line is a riddle. Read twice. What does it mean? The Seal remembers only the forgotten? I think it means the Seal's value is remembering the erased people. But as phrased: "It remembers everyone." "Not everyone. Only those the system was taught to forget." That's a contradiction dressed as profundity. Read twice, gave up slightly.

Page 31: Public square, names appear. Alpha: "Request denied. Foundational instrument has priority." So the Seal outranks Alpha? "Foundational instrument" — new term. Lock realizes the system isn't under House control.

Page 32: The choice: CLAIM SOLE INHERITANCE vs RESTORE CONTRIBUTOR OWNERSHIP. Alex presses RESTORE. "If I claim it all, I become exactly what they wanted." Good beat, though "what they wanted" — did they want him to claim it all? Lock wanted him to sign to the Houses. Claiming sole inheritance isn't quite what Lock wanted. Hmm, "exactly what they wanted" = a sole owner playing the ownership game. Eh. It lands okay emotionally.

Page 33: Montage caption: "The Maker's Seal did not make everyone equal. It made their contributions visible." Thesis caption again. It's a nice summary but it's the book grading its own homework.

Page 34: The Covenant record. "Adrian's and Mera's custodian marks are visible. A third mark remains sealed." Wait — Mera is a Covenant custodian? News. And "COLLABORATOR: So did Mera." — how does the collaborator know? Whatever. "THIRD CUSTODIAN: IDENTITY SEALED / LAST SHARED LOCATION: OASIS." "Someone both of them agreed the world should forget." Hook for issue 3.

Page 35: Mera on a display: "If you continue, the Covenant will ask more of you than the Seal did." Cryptic warning. Alex: "Good." — the "Good." is very action-hero. Slight eye-roll.

Page 36: The sealed identity field fills the page, and in the reflection, "the silhouette of a woman with Ada's copper hair and posture." — Oh. The third custodian is Ada's mother (or relative). That's the cliffhanger. It's a good one — I did not see it coming, and it recontextualizes Ada's rivet-rubbing (the brass rivet on her strap — mentioned page 3 and page 36 — her mother's? The rivet motif pays off as a tell). Actually wait, was the rivet established as connected to her mother? Page 3: "Ada rubs the brass rivet on her shoulder strap." Page 36: "Ada's thumb rubs the brass rivet." It's a tic. The silhouette reveal: woman with Ada's copper hair. So: Ada's mom. I predicted it the moment the reflection was described — well, the page tells you directly. It's a strong issue-ending hook. Yes I'd read issue 3.

Issue 2 put-down point: page 21's Lock scene (choppy, missing beats) or the caption-heavy page 20. The middle of issue 2 (pages 22-27) is a lot of talk about patents and ownership — for a 15-year-old, "intellectual estate," "312 patents," "ownership classifications may become contestable" — this is dry. The book becomes about IP law. I'd skim. Put-down candidate: page 21 or somewhere in 22-23.

**Issue 03 — Oasis (pages 37-54)**

Page 37: Oasis. "Oasis had learned how to provide almost everything. It had not learned how to belong to one another." — grammar: "how to belong to one another" — the city belongs to each other? Thesis caption, slightly off grammatically. Displaced Keel families behind eligibility lines. Okay.

Page 38: THIRD COVENANT CUSTODIAN: LEONA VEYRA. "That's my mother." Then: "I thought she was dead." / "I thought she left after she died." — read that twice. "I thought she left after she died"? That's a weird line. I think it's meant to be a flustered correction — "I thought she was dead... I mean, I thought she left, and then she died"? As written it's a riddle. Actually maybe: "I thought she left. After [that], she died [is what I believed]." The line as written is scrambled. Read twice, still not sure. Real finding — quote it.

Page 39: Leona. "You came farther than I expected." "I let you believe what kept you unmarked." "My silence for your protection." Okay — the bargain. Ada: "That isn't protection." Leona: "No. It was the bargain I could make." Decent confrontation, a bit aphoristic.

Page 40: Water Wars flashback. "During the Water Wars, the Covenant moved scarce water between communities." First use of "Water Wars" — the reader.md says students don't know what the water wars are until the book tells them. Page 40 is the first telling, and it's brief: reservoir fell, one community closed a gate, another forced it open, fear broke the agreement. Okay, minimal but sufficient. "And you decided people couldn't be trusted again."

Page 41: Mera's face first time. "The failure was not proof that people were evil. It was proof that panic makes decisions faster than accountability." — aphorism. Leona: "Mera called for emergency suspension of the Covenant. I agreed. He refused." Adrian refused. So the Covenant was suspended, Adrian held out. "Alpha was tracing everyone connected to Adrian. Mera suppressed your association risk." So Mera protected Ada by erasing her association. "My silence for your protection." Repeated. "You protected me from knowing you." Good line from Ada — lands.

Page 42: The three components: Leona's, Mera's (in the control system), Adrian's (in Alex's evidence case — wait, when did Alex get Adrian's Covenant component? Page 11: Bi11bot placed "three separate Covenant components" on the table in Keel. Hmm — "three separate Covenant components" were on Adrian's worktable? Then page 42 says the three components are in three places: Leona's apartment, Mera's control system, Alex's evidence case. If all three were on the table in Keel... no wait, page 11 says "three separate Covenant components" — maybe those were Adrian's? Or representations? Confusing. Page 11: "the brass-and-glass Measure, the interrupted-line Maker's Seal, and three separate Covenant components." So Adrian had three Covenant components?? But page 42 says each custodian held one: Leona, Mera, Adrian. So Adrian's component is in Alex's evidence case — when did Alex put it there? Presumably from the workshop. But page 11 showed THREE components. If the Covenant needs three custodians' components and Adrian had all three on his table, then... no. I think page 11's "three separate Covenant components" is meant to be Adrian's one component being in three pieces? "They only move when people do." Ugh. Ledger: Covenant components — page 11 shows three on the table; page 42 says they're held by three different people in three places. Contradiction or I misread. As a cold reader: confused. Also when did Alex acquire "Adrian's component" into an "evidence case"? The evidence case appears on page 42 with no setup. Actually page 50: "Alex stands before the evidence" and page 54 "the evidence case." The case is never introduced. Minor.

Page 43: Mera enters. "Give me the Measure and the Maker's Seal." Offers: Keel water, Halyard reviews, Oasis access — "Leave that buried" (the Covenant). "The offer is real." / "That's the problem." — this exact exchange repeats on page 52 ("MERA: The offer is real. ALEX: That's the problem."). Verbatim repeat. Intentional echo? Probably intentional, but as a cold reader it reads like a copy-paste. I'd notice. Hmm, it's clearly meant as a deliberate parallel (Mera's offer vs Alpha's offer).
